chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Baseer, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the man who says, 'Upon me is a vow.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not binding until he specifies the vow and says, 'Upon me is a fast for Allah,' or he gives charity, or frees a slave, or offers a gift. And if the man says, 'I gift this food,' then this is not binding; rather, the offering is the camel (or livestock).'

key_terms.الْبُدْنُ: Camels or livestock used for offering
key_terms.نَذْرٌ: Vow, a voluntary commitment to perform an act of worship or good deed for the sake of God
key_terms.هَدْياً: A gift offering, typically referring to livestock

ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for a vow to be considered binding in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the principle of specificity (takhshis) in vow-making, requiring the vow-taker to explicitly define the act to ensure legal enforceability. It further refines the terminology by distinguishing between general food offerings and the technical definition of 'hadya' (sacrificial animal), reflecting the juristic precision characteristic of Shia fiqh. This ruling underscores the importance of clear intention and specific commitment in fulfilling religious obligations voluntarily undertaken.
